Introduction¶

The goal of this project is to build a machine learning model that predicts whether a Formula 1 driver will finish on the podium, meaning in the top three, in a Grand Prix. This is therefor a Binary Classification, problem because each driver result is classified as either a podium finish or a non-podium finish.

The data for this project comes from the Formula 1 World Championship (1950–2024) dataset on Kaggle. It includes race results, drivers, lap times, and other relavent race-related data that would be helpfull to train the model to create accurate predictions. This data set includes many csv files, which can be joined with keys like raceID and driverID.

This dataset includes both categorical and numerical variables.

Numerical: grid position, finishing position, points, laps completed, qualifying rank, and standings points

Categorical: driver name, constructor/team, circuit, race name, nationality, and race status

How does Forumula 1 Work?¶

A F1 season is made up of multiple Grand Prix weekends. During this weeking, drivers participate in practice sessions, qualifying, and the main Grand Prix race.

There are three practice sessions where the driver and the team (constructor) prepare the car, but do not determine points or positions.

Qualifying determines a drivers starting position in the Grand Prix. It is brocken up into three sessions:

- Q1 (18 minutes): All 20 drivers race. The 6 slowest drivers are eliminated and fill grid positions 16 through 20
- Q2 (15 minutes): The remaining 14 drivers compete. The 6 slowest drivers are eliminated to secure grid positions 11 through 15. 
- Q3 (12 minutes): The final 10 drivers race to determine the top 10 starting spots for the Grand Prix.

The faster the driver, the lower their starting position is (pole position). Sometimes the final starting grid can differ from qualifying order because of penalties or car changes.

The Grand Prix is the main race. Drivers earn championship points based on their finishing position, and the top three finishers are considered podium finishers.

Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Before building the models, I explored and cleaned the datasets to better understand the data and which variables can be useful. In this section I will look at the overall structure of the data, check distributions and visualize imporant predictors like grid position, qualifying position, standings, and constructor performance. This helps identify patterns in the data and gives context for which variables may be useful in predicting podium finishes.

podium_counts

finish_type count

Wow! This table shows that this dataset is highly imbalanced. Most observates are non-podium finishes, with ~23k Not Podium and ~3.4k Podium. The model can be correct by predicting non-podium, which isn't useful to predict podium drivers. Therefor accuracy alone can be misleading, metrics like ROC-AUC, precision, recall, and F1-score are also needed

Merge dataset into one master dataset¶

Since the original Formula 1 data is stored across multiple separate tables, merging the relevant files into one master dataset would be beneficial for modeling and analysis. This step is necessary because the outcome variable comes from the race results table, while important predictors such as driver information, constructor information, circuit details, qualifying position, and standings come from different tables.

Each table contains key columns such as raceId, driverId, constructorId, circuitId, and statusId. I used these keys to merge the tables together, which ensures that each driver, race, constructor, circuit, and race status is matched correctly.

In [7]:
df = results.copy()

df = df.merge(races, on="raceId", how="left", suffixes=("", "_race"))
df = df.merge(drivers, on="driverId", how="left", suffixes=("", "_driver"))
df = df.merge(constructors, on="constructorId", how="left", suffixes=("", "_constructor"))
df = df.merge(circuits, on="circuitId", how="left", suffixes=("", "_circuit"))
df = df.merge(status, on="statusId", how="left")


df = df.rename(columns={
    "name": "race_name",
    "url": "race_url",
    "time_race": "race_time",
    "name_constructor": "constructor_name",
    "nationality_constructor": "constructor_nationality",
    "url_constructor": "constructor_url",
    "name_circuit": "circuit_name",
    "url_circuit": "circuit_url",
    "location": "circuit_location",
    "country": "circuit_country"
})

new_qualifying = qualifying[[

df = df.merge(

Add Pit Stop Data¶

  • number of pit stops
  • mean times
  • total pit stop time for that race
In [12]:
pit_features = (
    pit_stops
    .groupby(["raceId", "driverId"])
    .agg(
        num_pit_stops=("stop", "count"),
        avg_pit_stop_ms=("milliseconds", "mean"),
        total_pit_stop_ms=("milliseconds", "sum")
    )
    .reset_index()
)

df = df.merge(
    pit_features,
    on=["raceId", "driverId"],
    how="left"
)
In [13]:
#fill in missing pit stop data
df["num_pit_stops"] = df["num_pit_stops"].fillna(0)

Add Lap Times¶

lap_features = (
    lap_times

    .agg(
        avg_lap_ms=("milliseconds", "mean"),
        best_lap_ms=("milliseconds", "min"),

    )
    .reset_index()
)

df = df.merge(

    on=["raceId", "driverId"],

)

Number of Races Over Time¶

In [20]:
races = pd.read_csv("../data/races.csv")

races_per_year = (
    races
    .groupby("year")
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="num_races")
)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))

sns.lineplot(
    data=races_per_year,
    x="year",
    y="num_races",
    linewidth=1.9,
    color="#E10600"
)

plt.title("Number of Formula 1 Grands Prix per Season", fontsize=16, weight="bold")
plt.xlabel("Season")
plt.ylabel("Number of Races")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This plot shows how the Formula 1 calendar has changed over time. Earlier seasons had fewer races, while modern seasons include more Grands Prix. This matters because recent seasons contribute more observations to the dataset.

The increase in races also show that older seasons may not reflect the same racing environment as modern seasons. The model may learn more useful patterns from more recent season where teams, qualifying structure, and overall competition are more similar to present day.

Podium vs non-podium distribution¶

In [21]:
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))

sns.barplot(
    data=podium_counts,
    x="finish_type",
    y="count",
    hue="finish_type",
    palette={
        "Not Podium": "#1f1f1f",
        "Podium": "#E10600"
    },
    legend=False
)

plt.title("Distribution of Podium vs Non-Podium Finishes")
plt.xlabel("Finish Type")
plt.ylabel("Number of Driver-Race Results")
plt.show()

This plot shows that podium finishes are much less common than non-podium finishes. This class imbalance is expected because only three drivers can finish on the podium. Therefor, accuracy alone is not enough to evaluate the models.

Podium Rate by Qualifying Position¶

In [22]:
plt.figure(figsize=(9,5))

eda_df = df.copy()

eda_df["podium"] = (eda_df["positionOrder"] <= 3).astype(int)

eda_df["podium_label"] = eda_df["podium"].map({
    1: "Podium",
    0: "Not Podium"
})


qual_podium = (
    eda_df
    .dropna(subset=["qualifying_position"])
    .groupby("qualifying_position")
    .agg(
        starts=("podium", "count"),
        podium_rate=("podium", "mean")
    )
    .reset_index()
)


sns.lineplot(
    data=qual_podium,
    x="qualifying_position",
    y="podium_rate",
    marker="o",
    linewidth=2.5,
    color="#E10600"
)

plt.title("Podium Rate by Qualifying Position", fontsize=16, weight="bold")
plt.xlabel("Qualifying Position")
plt.ylabel("Podium Rate")
plt.xticks(qual_podium["qualifying_position"])
plt.ylim(0, 1)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This plot shows that starting position is strongly related to podium finishes. Drivers whose starting position is near the front of the grid have a much higher podium rate than drivers starting further back.

Since podium rate drops sharply after the first few starting positions, qualifying position shuold be used as one of the main predictors in the model. However, race outcomes can still be affected by strategy, reliability, penalties, crashes, weather, and team performance. Therefor qualifying position is important, but it should be combined with other pre-race variables rather than used alone.

)

constructor_podium = constructor_podium[constructor_podium["starts"] >= 20]
constructor_podium = constructor_podium.sort_values("podium_rate", ascending=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

colors = constructor_podium["constructor_name"].map(team_colors).fillna("#999999")

ax.barh(
    constructor_podium["constructor_name"],
    constructor_podium["podium_rate"],
    color=colors
)

ax.set_title("Modern Constructor Podium Rates", fontsize=16, weight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("Podium Rate")
ax.set_ylabel("Constructor")
ax.invert_yaxis()

for i, row in constructor_podium.reset_index(drop=True).iterrows():
    team = row["constructor_name"]
    logo_path = logo_paths.get(team)

    if logo_path is not None and os.path.exists(logo_path):
        img = mpimg.imread(logo_path)
        imagebox = OffsetImage(img, zoom=0.08)
        ab = AnnotationBbox(
            imagebox,
            (row["podium_rate"] + 0.025, i),
            frameon=False
        )
        ax.add_artist(ab)

ax.set_xlim(0, constructor_podium["podium_rate"].max() + 0.15)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This plot compares podium rates across Formula 1 constructors from 2020 onwards. It indicates that certain teams tend to have much higher podium rates. Red Bull, Mercedes and Ferrari seem to dominate the sport which could be a good indicator for predicting if a driver achieves a podium standing.

This is useful for the model because a driver’s chance of finishing on the podium depends not only on the driver, but also on the strength of the car and team. Constructors with stronger cars are more likely to finish in the top three. Because of this, constructor-related variables are important predictors for podium classification as well.

Before Race Data¶

Some variables in this dataset are only known during or after race, such as final position, points, pit stops, lap times, race status, fastest lap information, and race-level constructor points. These variables will not be used in the final pre-race prediction model because they would cause data leakage.

Driver points before race vs podium¶

In [116]:
points_df = df[df["year"] >= 2020].copy()

points_df["driver_points_tier"] = pd.cut(
    points_df["driver_points_before_race"],
    bins=[-1, 0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600],
    labels=[
        "0",
        "1-10",
        "11-25",
        "26-50",
        "51-100",
        "101-200",
        "201-400",
        "400+"
    ]
)

points_summary = (
    points_df
    .groupby("driver_points_tier", observed=True)
    .agg(
        starts=("podium", "count"),
        podium_rate=("podium", "mean"),
        avg_points=("driver_points_before_race", "mean")
    )
    .reset_index()
)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))

sns.barplot(
    data=points_summary,
    x="driver_points_tier",
    y="podium_rate",
    color="#E10600"
)

plt.title("Podium Rate by Driver Points Before Race", fontsize=16, weight="bold")
plt.xlabel("Driver Points Before Race")
plt.ylabel("Podium Rate")
plt.ylim(0, 1)

for i, row in points_summary.iterrows():
    plt.text(
        i,
        row["podium_rate"] + 0.02,
        f'n={row["starts"]}',
        ha="center",
        fontsize=9
    )

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This plot shows that drivers with more points before a race are much more likely to finish on the podium. Drivers with 0 or 1–10 points before a race have very low podium rates, while drivers with 201–400 points have a podium rate above 50%.

Overall, this supports using driver_points_before_race as a predictor because it captures current-season driver performance before the race begins. However, the sample sizes shown above the bars also show that very high point totals are rare, so the model should not rely only on this variable.

In [45]:
cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=42
)

Because Formula 1 data is time-based, I used a chronological split instead of a random split. I am using races from 2020 - 2024 as the final test set and earlier races for model training and validation.

And in the training data, I used stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Stratification is useful because podium finishes are much less common than non-podium finishes, so each fold should keep a similar class balance.

Define Models:¶

models = {

    #baseline
    "Logistic Regression": make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000, random_state=42)
    ),

    "Elastic Net Logistic Regression": make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        LogisticRegression(
            solver="saga",
            l1_ratio=0.5,
            C=1.0,
            max_iter=5000,
            random_state=42
        )
    ),

    "LDA": make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        LinearDiscriminantAnalysis()
    ),

    "QDA": make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis(reg_param=0.1)
    ),

    "KNN": make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15)
    ),

    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(
        max_depth=5,
        random_state=42
    ),

    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=200,
        random_state=42,
        class_weight="balanced"
    ),

    "Gradient Boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(
        random_state=42
    )
}

Test loop¶

In [48]:
cv_results = []

scoring = {
    "accuracy": "accuracy",
    "precision": "precision",
    "recall": "recall",
    "f1": "f1",
    "roc_auc": "roc_auc"
}

for feature_set_name, features in feature_sets.items():
    
    X_train = train[features]
    y_train = train["podium"]
    
    for model_name, model in models.items():
        
        scores = cross_validate(
            model,
            X_train,
            y_train,
            cv=cv,
            scoring=scoring,
            n_jobs=-1
        )
        
        cv_results.append({
            "feature_set": feature_set_name,
            "model": model_name,
            "accuracy": scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
            "precision": scores["test_precision"].mean(),
            "recall": scores["test_recall"].mean(),
            "f1": scores["test_f1"].mean(),
            "roc_auc": scores["test_roc_auc"].mean()
        })

results_df = pd.DataFrame(cv_results)

tuned_results = []
best_tuned_models = {}

for model_name, setup in tuning_models.items():
    
    print("Tuning:", model_name)
    
    grid_search = GridSearchCV(
        estimator=setup["model"],
        param_grid=setup["params"],
        scoring="roc_auc",
        cv=cv,
        n_jobs=-1
    )
    
    grid_search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    
    best_tuned_models[model_name] = grid_search
    
    tuned_results.append({
        "model": model_name,
        "best_cv_roc_auc": grid_search.best_score_,
        "best_params": grid_search.best_params_
    })

tuned_results_df = pd.DataFrame(tuned_results)

The models with meaningful hyperparameters were tuned using 5-fold stratified cross-validation. KNN was tuned over the number of neighbors and weighting method, Decision Tree was tuned over maximum depth and minimum leaf size, Random Forest was tuned over number of trees, maximum depth, minimum leaf size, and number of features considered at each split, and Gradient Boosting was tuned over number of estimators, learning rate, and tree depth. The model with the highest cross-validated ROC-AUC was selected as the final model.

from matplotlib.patches import Patch

def plot_race_predictions(year, round_num, race_name):
    
    one_race = (
        test_predictions[(test_predictions["year"] == year) & (test_predictions["round"] == round_num)]
        .sort_values("predicted_podium_probability", ascending=False)
        .head(10)
        .copy()
    )

    one_race["driver_name"] = one_race["forename"] + " " + one_race["surname"]

    colors = one_race["predicted_podium_top3"].map({
        1: "#E10600",
        0: "#B6BABD"
    })

    plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))

    plt.barh(
        one_race["driver_name"],
        one_race["predicted_podium_probability"],
        color=colors,
        edgecolor="black",
        linewidth=1
    )

    plt.gca().invert_yaxis()

    #star actual podium finishers
    for position, (_, row) in enumerate(one_race.iterrows()):
        if row["podium"] == 1:
            plt.text(
                row["predicted_podium_probability"] + 0.015,
                position,
                "★ Actual Podium",
                va="center",
                fontsize=10,
                weight="bold",
                color="#FFD700"
            )

    plt.title(f"Top Predicted Podium Contenders for {race_name}",
              fontsize=16, weight="bold")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted Podium Probability")
    plt.ylabel("Driver")

    legend_items = [
        Patch(facecolor="#E10600", edgecolor="black", label="Model Predicted Top 3"),
        Patch(facecolor="#B6BABD", edgecolor="black", label="Outside Predicted Top 3"),
    ]

    plt.legend(handles=legend_items, title="Legend", loc="lower right")

    sns.despine()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
